questions.stem:
The Venn diagram shows the probability of a randomly selected student from a school being in the sets $L$, $B$ and $C$, where
$L$ represents the event that the student has instrumental music lessons
$B$ represents the event that the student plays in the school band
$C$ represents the event that the student sings in the school choir
$p$, $q$, $r$ and $s$ are probabilities.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Select a pair of mutually exclusive events from $L$, $B$ and $C$.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: B1: $B$ and $C$ or "band" and "choir" but NOT $\mathrm{P}(B)$ and $\mathrm{P}(C)$. Note: B1 for $B$ and $C$ indicated. Allow other non-trivial pairs e.g. $B$ and $L\cap C$ but not $L$ and $L'$

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Given that $\mathrm{P}(L) = 0.4$, $\mathrm{P}(B) = 0.13$, $\mathrm{P}(C) = 0.3$ and the events $L$ and $C$ are independent,
(b) find the value of $p$,
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: [$L$ and $C$ independent implies] $\mathrm{P}(L\cap C)=\mathrm{P}(L)\times\mathrm{P}(C)=0.4\times0.3$
A1: $p=0.12$
Correct answers only to parts (b), (c) or (d) score all the relevant marks.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1 for clear attempt to use the rule for independence. Rule stated and one correct sub.
- A1 for 0.12 (either labelled $p$ or part (b) or correctly placed on Venn diagram)

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) find the value of $q$, the value of $r$ and the value of $s$.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
1st B1ft: $q=0.4-0.13-\text{their }p=0.15$ or a correct $q$ allowing ft of their $p$
2nd B1ft: $r=0.3-\text{their }p=0.18$ or a correct $r$ allowing ft of their $p$
3rd B1ft: $s=1-(0.4+0.3-\text{their }p)$ or $1-(0.4+\text{their }r)=0.42$ or a correct $s$ allowing ft of their $p$ or $r$. The ft requires all values concerned to be probabilities.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- The ft requires all values concerned to be probabilities. (Labelled or on Venn diagram)
- Accept probabilities in any exact form e.g. $\frac{3}{20}$ for 0.15 or $\frac{3}{25}$ for 0.12 etc

parts.label: d
parts.text:
A student is selected at random from those who play in the school band or sing in the school choir.
(d) Find the exact probability that this student has instrumental music lessons.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: for a correct probability expression $\mathrm{P}(L\mid B\cup C)$ or $\frac{\mathrm{P}(L\cap[B\cup C])}{\mathrm{P}(B\cup C)}=\frac{0.13+"0.12"}{0.13+0.3}$ and any ratio of probabilities (num < denom). May be implied by a correct (or correct ft) probability ratio.
1st A1ft: for a correct (or correct ft) probability ratio (num < denom)
2nd A1: $=\frac{25}{43}$ or exact equivalent. NB completed Venn diagram. (If answers conflict the script takes preference over diagram)

questions.stem: The weights of women boxers in a tournament are normally distributed with mean 64 kg and standard deviation 8 kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen woman boxer in the tournament weighs less than 51 kg.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
$[W\sim \mathrm{N}(64,8^2)]$
M1: standardising with 51 (or 77), 64 and 8 (allow $\pm$): $\mathrm{P}(W<51)=\mathrm{P}\left(Z<\frac{51-64}{8}\right)$ or $\mathrm{P}(Z<-1.625)$. Implied by $z=$ awrt $\pm 1.62/3$
M1: for $1-p$ where $0.9<p<1$
A1: $=1-0.9484$ (calc. $1-0.9479187299...$) = awrt $\mathbf{0.052}$ (NB If they use $z=(\pm)1.62$ from correct standardising allow 0.053). Calculator gives $0.0520812...$ [ans only of awrt 0.052 is 3/3]

parts.label: b
parts.text:
In the tournament, women boxers who weigh less than 51 kg are classified as lightweight. Ren weighs 49 kg and she has a match against another randomly selected, lightweight woman boxer.
(b) Find the probability that Ren weighs less than the other boxer.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
Require: $\mathrm{P}(W>49\mid W<51)$
1st M1: for a correctly stated conditional probability. May be implied by correct ratio: $=\frac{\mathrm{P}(49<W<51)}{\mathrm{P}(W<51)}$ or $\frac{\mathrm{P}(-1.875<Z<-1.625)}{\mathrm{P}(Z<-1.625)}$
2nd M1: for a correct ratio of probabilities in their $W$ or $Z$ (either version from scheme). $\frac{(a)-\mathrm{P}(W<49)}{(a)}$ or $1-\frac{\mathrm{P}(W<49)}{(a)}$ will score M1M1
1st A1ft: for a correct ratio of probabilities with their (a) on denominator and numerator in the range [0.0215, 0.0219]. Num > Denom is A0. $=\frac{0.021684...}{(a)}$
2nd A1: for a final answer of awrt 0.42 (dep on at least one other mark). $=0.4163...$ awrt $\mathbf{0.42}$. Final answer of $\frac{5}{12}$ will lose the final A1 unless awrt 0.42 is seen as well. Ans only: For an answer of 0.416 or better award 4/4

parts.label: c
parts.text:
In the tournament, women boxers who weigh more than $H$ kg are classified as heavyweight. Given that 10% of the women boxers in the tournament are classified as heavyweight,
(c) find the value of $H$.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: for standardising with $H$, 64 and 8 and setting equal to a $z$ value where $|z|>1$: $\left[\mathrm{P}(W>H)=0.10\Rightarrow\right]\frac{H-64}{8}=1.2816$
B1: for using $z=\pm1.2816$ (or better e.g. calc: $1.2815515...$) can be with $8^2$ instead of 8 etc. $\mathrm{P}\left(Z>\frac{H-64}{8}\right)=1.2816$ can score M1B0 unless a correct answer implies 3/3
A1: for awrt 74.3 (calc gives $74.25241253...$). Award M1B0A1 for an answer of 74.24 or awrt 74.2 if B0 scored for $z=1.28$. Ans only for an answer only of awrt 74.3 (can come from $z=1.282$ etc) award M1B0A1. Ans only for an answer for $H$ in the range $74.252\leqslant H\leqslant 74.253$ award M1B1A1

questions.stem:
A group of 100 adults recorded the amount of time, $t$ minutes, they spent exercising each day. Their results are summarised in the table below.
$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Time }(t\text{ minutes}) & \text{Frequency }(f) & \text{Time midpoint }(x)\\\hline 0 \leqslant t < 15 & 25 & 7.5\\\hline 15 \leqslant t < 30 & 17 & 22.5\\\hline 30 \leqslant t < 60 & 28 & 45\\\hline 60 \leqslant t < 120 & 24 & 90\\\hline 120 \leqslant t \leqslant 240 & 6 & 180\\\hline\end{array}$
$[\text{You may use } \sum fx^2 = 455512.5]$
A histogram is drawn to represent these data.
The bar representing the time $0 \leqslant t < 15$ has width 0.5 cm and height 6 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Calculate the width and height of the bar representing a time of $60 \leqslant t < 120$
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: Width: 15 minutes is 0.5 cm so 60 mins will be $4\times0.5=2$ (cm)
M1: Height: freq of 25 represented by $6\times0.5=3$ (cm$^2$) so freq of 24 is $\frac{24}{25}\times3$
A1: So height $=\frac{1}{"2"}\times\frac{24}{25}\times3=1.44$ (cm) (or exact equivalent e.g. $\frac{36}{25}$)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1 for some calc' linking area and frequency for both groups or their $w\times$their $h=2.88$

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Use linear interpolation to estimate the median time spent exercising by these adults each day.
(2)

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) Find an estimate of the mean time spent exercising by these adults each day.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Use of midpoints to get $\sum fx=5070$ (allow 5000 to 1sf) or a fully correct expression using midpoints
A1: $[\bar{t}$ or $\bar{x}]=50.7$ or exact equivalent e.g. $\frac{5070}{100}$

parts.label: d
parts.text:
(d) Calculate an estimate for the standard deviation of these times.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: for a correct expression including square root (ft their mean): $[\sigma]=\sqrt{\frac{455512.5}{100}-"50.7"^2}$ or $\sqrt{1984.635}$
A1: for awrt 44.5 (or 44.55) (allow use of $s=44.77367...$ or awrt 44.8). $=44.5492...$ awrt $\mathbf{44.5}$

parts.label: e
parts.text:
(e) Describe, giving a reason, the skewness of these data.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: B1: for positive skew plus a suitable correct reason [allow use of values provided (c) > (b)]. $\bar{t}$ or $\bar{x}>Q_2$ [allow "50.7">"38.6" or formula] so positive (skew). Allow correct use of quartiles but must see $Q_1=15$ and $Q_3=72.5$

parts.label: f
parts.text:
Further analysis of the above data revealed that 18 of the 25 adults in the $0 \leqslant t < 15$ group took no exercise each day.
(f) State, giving a reason, what effect, if any, this new information would have on your answers to
(i) the estimate of the median in part (b),
(ii) the estimate of the mean in part (c),
(iii) the estimate of the standard deviation in part (d).
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
B2: for all 3 correct statements  B1: for only 2 correct statements (B1B0). 3rd B1 dep on B2 for at least one suitable reason. (Allow calculation of $\bar{x}$ or $\sigma$ or $s$). Do not accept comments like "median not affected by extreme values"
(i) Median: no change. Since e.g. all 18 values or all changes are still below the median
(ii) Mean: will be smaller. Since e.g. changes will reduce total of $x$ ($7\times7.5$ not $25\times7.5$ in 1st class)
(iii) Standard deviation: will be greater. Since e.g. (18 zeros means) data more spread out
NB With 18 zeros $\Sigma fx=4935$, $\bar{x}=49.35$, $\Sigma fx^2=454500$, $\sigma=45.930...$, $s=46.161...$

questions.stem:
Some children are playing a game involving throwing a ball into a bucket. Each child has 3 throws and the number of times the ball lands in the bucket, $x$, is recorded. Their results are given in the table below.
$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3\\\hline \text{Frequency} & 16 & 36 & 24 & 4\\\hline\end{array}$

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Sandra decides to model the game by assuming that on each throw, the probability of the ball landing in the bucket is 0.4 for every child on every throw and that the throws are all independent. The random variable $S$ represents the number of times the ball lands in the bucket for a randomly selected child.
(b) Find $\mathrm{P}(S=2)$
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
Mark (b) and (c) together (M1 is for a full method for $\mathrm{P}(S=2)$)
M1: for $k\times0.4^2\times0.6$ (including $k=1$) where $k\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ or $3\times p^2\times(1-p)$ for some $p\in(0,1)$: $\mathrm{P}(S=2)=3\times0.4^2\times0.6$
A1: $=0.288$ or an exact equivalent e.g. $\frac{36}{125}$. Correct answers in table can score all marks in (b) and (c). Table takes preference.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) Complete the table below to show the probability distribution for $S$.
$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline s & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3\\\hline \mathrm{P}(S=s) & & 0.432 & & 0.064\\\hline\end{array}$
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: B1ft: for $\mathrm{P}(S=0)=1-(0.496+"0.288")$ or $0.6^3=0.216$ based on sum of probabilities = 1

parts.label: d
parts.text:
Ting believes that the probability of the ball landing in the bucket is not the same for each throw. He suggests that the probability will increase with each throw and uses the model
$p_i = 0.15i+0.10$
where $i=1,2,3$ and $p_i$ is the probability that the $i$th throw of the ball, by any particular child, will land in the bucket.
The random variable $T$ represents the number of times the ball lands in the bucket for a randomly selected child using Ting's model.
(d) Show that
(i) $\mathrm{P}(T=3)=0.055$
(ii) $\mathrm{P}(T=1)=0.45$
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
1st M1: for a correct attempt to find all 3 $p_i$ values. Implied by the correct product expr': $p_1=0.25$ and $p_2=0.4$ and $p_3=0.55$
1st A1: for a correct numerical product and no incorrect working seen for $\mathrm{P}(T=3)$: $\mathrm{P}(T=3)=p_1\times p_2\times p_3=0.25\times0.4\times0.55=0.055$ (*)
2nd M1: for at least 1 correct product in $\mathrm{P}(T=1)$ (ft their $p_i$ probabilities)
2nd A1: for at least 2 correct products seen: $\mathrm{P}(T=1)=0.25\times0.6\times0.45+0.75\times0.4\times0.45+0.75\times0.6\times0.55$ or $=0.0675+0.135+0.2475$. Beware: $(1-p_3)=0.45$ is 2nd M0
3rd A1cso: for all 3 correct products seen and no incorrect working seen: $=0.45$ (*)

parts.label: e
parts.text:
(e) Complete the table below to show the probability distribution for $T$, stating the exact probabilities in each case.
$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline t & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3\\\hline \mathrm{P}(T=t) & & 0.45 & & 0.055\\\hline\end{array}$
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: for a correct product for $\mathrm{P}(T=0)$ or all 3 correct products for $\mathrm{P}(T=2)$ (ft their $p_i$): $\mathrm{P}(T=0)=0.75\times0.6\times0.45$ (or equivalent expression for $\mathrm{P}(T=2)$)
1st A1: for either correct probability (correctly labelled or placed in the table): $=0.2025$ (Allow $\frac{81}{400}$)
2nd A1ft: for a correct 4th probability or a 4th probability in the table that makes the sum = 1: $\mathrm{P}(T=2)=1-(0.505+"0.2025")=0.2925$ (Allow $\frac{117}{400}$). Correct answers in table can score all marks in (e). Table takes preference.

parts.label: f
parts.text:
(f) State, giving your reasons, whether Sandra's model or Ting's model is the more appropriate for modelling this game.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: for attempt at calculating probs from the data or freqs $S(f)$ and $T(f)$ (at least 3 correct)
1st A1: for all figs correct (2sf) and comparison of probs (or frequencies) for the 2 models
2nd A1: for clearly choosing Ting's model (dependent on M1A1 scored) e.g. "Ting's is best because probabilities (or frequencies) are always closer" scores A1A1
SC (A0A0): B1 choose Ting because probs improve or lack of independence etc (M0A1A0 or M1A1A0)

(b) Find $\mathrm{P}(S=2)$
(2)
(c) Complete the table below to show the probability distribution for $S$.
$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline s & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3\\\hline \mathrm{P}(S=s) & & 0.432 & & 0.064\\\hline\end{array}$
(1)
Ting believes that the probability of the ball landing in the bucket is not the same for each throw. He suggests that the probability will increase with each throw and uses the model
$p_i = 0.15i+0.10$
where $i=1,2,3$ and $p_i$ is the probability that the $i$th throw of the ball, by any particular child, will land in the bucket.
The random variable $T$ represents the number of times the ball lands in the bucket for a randomly selected child using Ting's model.
(d) Show that
(i) $\mathrm{P}(T=3)=0.055$
(ii) $\mathrm{P}(T=1)=0.45$
(5)
(e) Complete the table below to show the probability distribution for $T$, stating the exact probabilities in each case.
$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline t & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3\\\hline \mathrm{P}(T=t) & & 0.45 & & 0.055\\\hline\end{array}$
(3)
(f) State, giving your reasons, whether Sandra's model or Ting's model is the more appropriate for modelling this game.
(3)
